newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan key discount rate seen flat until end-Sept.
newsitem.headline: Japan key discount rate seen flat until end-Sept.

text.p: Japan's key official discount rate is likely to be kept unchanged at the current record-low level until at least the end of September, leading economists predicted in a Reuters poll released on Thursday.

Of 26 economists at research institutes, banks and brokerages in Tokyo and London who responded to questions on interest rates, all but one expected the Bank of Japan (BOJ) to leave the discount rate unchanged at 0.5 percent until that time. The central bank charges the rate on loans to commercial banks.
The survey was conducted from April 1 to April 4 and covered 33 brokerages and research bodies, although not all those polled responded to all the questions.

The BOJ will need to wait until at least the end of September to evaluate the effect of the government's tight fiscal policy on the economy, said Takao Oshita, economist for Wako Research Institute of Economics Inc.
"The extent of the minus effects on the economy from a rise in the consumption tax and an end to special income tax cuts will only become clear at around October," said Oshita.
The government raised the consumption tax to five percent from three percent on April 1, when it also discontinued special income tax cuts.

Oshita said the BOJ would probably be able to raise the discount rate by 0.5 percentage point to 1.0 percent after September, when it would probably be able to confirm through economic data that the economy was on its way to an autonomous recovery.

Richard Werner, chief economist for Jardine Fleming Securities (Asia) Ltd, predicted that the BOJ would be able to raise the rate after September, as the strength of the economy would be clear by then.
"I think it will become clear that Japan will be able to achieve a nominal GDP growth of 3.3 percent and a growth of 2.5 percent in GDP in real terms," Werner said.
He said that the effect of the rise in the consumption tax on the economy was likely to be limited, and the pace of the economy's recovery would probably pick up in coming months.
"The net effect on the economy of the rise in the consumption tax will be small, because the negative effects of the rise will likely be offset by a recovery in the labour market," Werner said.

Susumu Kato, chief economist at BZW Securities Japan and the only economist surveyed who predicted the BOJ would raise the discount rate before the end of September, said the current level of Japanese interest rates was too low.
Kato said the results of the BOJ's next key survey of corporate sentiment, know as the "tankan", due out in July, would probably show a better-than-expected recovery in the economy.
Kato said he felt there was a disparity between business sentiment of non-manufacturers as revealed in the most recent "tankan" and actual economic conditions.
In that survey released on April 2, the key March diffusion index (DI) for major non-manufacturers came in at -6 while the DI for small non-manufacturers came in at -9.

The tankan indices, based on questionnaires circulated to companies, represent the percentage of firms which see business conditions as favourable minus those that see them as unfavourable. The higher the number, the better the outlook.

Kato said the easing of worries about deflation, and a recent rise in U.S. interest rates, would also make it easier for the BOJ to raise interest rates. He predicted that the central bank would raise the discount rate to 1.0 percent in the July-September quarter.
